prompt: Select the pin marking the Panama Canal, which links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
explanation: The Panama Canal cuts across the Isthmus of Panama in Central America, shortening sea routes between the Atlantic and Pacific.

trap_notes.default: Look for the narrow land bridge between North and South America.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Suez region linking the Mediterranean and Red Seas.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Strait of Malacca in Southeast Asia.
trap_notes.p4: That is Cape Horn at the southern tip of South America.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Amazon Basin, home to Earth's largest tropical rainforest.
explanation: The Amazon Basin spans northern South America along the Equator, draining vast tropical rainforests into the Atlantic Ocean.

trap_notes.default: Tropical rainforests cluster along the Equator; the Amazon is in South America.
trap_notes.p1: That marks the Congo Basin in central Africa.
trap_notes.p3: That marks the Indonesian archipelago in Southeast Asia.
trap_notes.p4: That marks temperate grasslands in central North America.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Sahara, the largest hot desert biome on Earth.
explanation: The Sahara stretches across northern Africa under a subtropical high-pressure belt around 20 to 30 degrees north latitude.

trap_notes.default: Look for the broad desert belt spanning northern Africa.
trap_notes.p2: That marks the Australian Outback.
trap_notes.p3: That marks the Gobi Desert in East Asia.
trap_notes.p4: That marks the Kalahari and Namib region in southern Africa.

prompt: Select the pin on the Gulf Stream, the warm current that moderates Western Europe's climate.
explanation: The Gulf Stream carries warm water northeastward across the North Atlantic, keeping Western Europe milder than similar latitudes.

trap_notes.default: Follow the warm current flowing northeast from Florida toward Europe.

trap_notes.p3: That is in the Indian Ocean basin.
trap_notes.p4: That is in the South Atlantic, south of the Equator.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Andes, the longest continental mountain range on Earth.
explanation: The Andes run along South America's entire western coast, formed by the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath South America.

trap_notes.default: Look along the western Pacific edge of South America.
trap_notes.p1: That marks the Rocky Mountains in North America.
trap_notes.p3: That marks the Alps in Europe.
trap_notes.p4: That marks the Himalayas in Asia.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system.
explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along Australia's northeastern coast in warm, shallow Coral Sea waters.

trap_notes.default: Find the northeastern coastline of Australia.

trap_notes.p3: That is off the coast of Madagascar and East Africa.
trap_notes.p4: That is near Japan in the temperate northwest Pacific.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Strait of Gibraltar, connecting the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.
explanation: The Strait of Gibraltar separates southern Spain from northern Morocco at the western entrance to the Mediterranean Sea.

trap_notes.default: Look at the far western outlet of the Mediterranean Sea.

trap_notes.p3: That is the Strait of Messina near Sicily.
trap_notes.p4: That is the Isthmus of Suez leading toward the Red Sea.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Suez Canal, which links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.
explanation: Opened in 1869, the Suez Canal crosses Egypt's Isthmus of Suez, allowing ships to bypass Africa between Europe and Asia.

trap_notes.default: Look in the southeastern corner of the Mediterranean east of the Nile.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Strait of Gibraltar at the Atlantic entrance.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Bosporus Strait leading to the Black Sea.
trap_notes.p4: That is in the Aegean Sea between Greece and Anatolia.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Bosporus Strait, the chokepoint linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
explanation: The Bosporus cuts through northwestern Turkey, connecting the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and the Aegean Sea.

trap_notes.default: Look for the narrow outlet at the southwestern corner of the Black Sea.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Adriatic Sea east of Italy.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Suez Canal region in Egypt.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Nile River Delta, where Africa's longest river meets the sea.
explanation: The Nile flows northward through Egypt and fans into a fertile triangular delta on the southeastern Mediterranean coast.

trap_notes.default: Follow the river flowing north out of Africa into the eastern Mediterranean.

trap_notes.p3: That is on the Italian Peninsula in southern Europe.
trap_notes.p4: That marks the island of Cyprus.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Italian Peninsula, which divides the western and eastern Mediterranean.
explanation: The Italian Peninsula juts southeast into the central Mediterranean toward Sicily, separating the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic Seas.

trap_notes.default: Look for the central boot-shaped peninsula pointing toward Sicily.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Iberian Peninsula in the far west.
trap_notes.p3: That is Greece on the southern Balkan Peninsula.
trap_notes.p4: That is Anatolia in modern-day Turkey.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Tigris-Euphrates river valley of Mesopotamia.
explanation: The Tigris and Euphrates flow southeast across Mesopotamia toward the Persian Gulf, forming the eastern Fertile Crescent.

trap_notes.default: Look east of the Mediterranean coast for the twin rivers flowing southeast.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Nile River in Egypt.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Black Sea north of Anatolia.
trap_notes.p4: That is the island of Crete.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Mississippi River Delta on the northern Gulf Coast.
explanation: The Mississippi River drains most of interior North America southward into a major delta along the northern Gulf of Mexico.

trap_notes.default: Follow the central north-south river all the way to the Gulf Coast.

trap_notes.p3: That is along the Atlantic coast, not the Gulf of Mexico.
trap_notes.p4: That is Lake Superior in the north.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Appalachian Mountains, the older eroded range in eastern North America.
explanation: The Appalachians run southwest to northeast parallel to the Atlantic coast, historically acting as a barrier to early westward settlement.

trap_notes.default: Look for the dashed mountain ridge running along eastern North America.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Rocky Mountain region in the west.
trap_notes.p3: That is the flat interior Great Plains.
trap_notes.p4: That is the low-lying Florida Peninsula.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Rocky Mountains, which form North America's Continental Divide.
explanation: The Rocky Mountains stretch down western North America, separating rivers flowing toward the Pacific from those flowing east.

trap_notes.default: Look in western North America near the headwaters of eastward-flowing rivers.
trap_notes.p2: That marks the Appalachian Mountains in the east.
trap_notes.p3: That marks the Great Lakes region.
trap_notes.p4: That marks the Yucatan Peninsula in the south.

prompt: Select the pin marking Lake Superior, the largest and northernmost of the five Great Lakes.
explanation: Lake Superior sits at the northwestern head of the Great Lakes system, holding more freshwater than the other four lakes combined.

trap_notes.default: Find the largest, farthest-northwest lake in the Great Lakes cluster.
trap_notes.p2: That is Lake Ontario at the eastern end.
trap_notes.p3: That is Lake Michigan extending southward.
trap_notes.p4: That is Lake Erie on the southern side.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Rio Grande, a river forming a major natural border in southern North America.
explanation: The Rio Grande flows southeast from the southern Rockies to the Gulf of Mexico, forming a natural border between Texas and Mexico.

trap_notes.default: Look in the southwest for the river flowing southeast into the Gulf of Mexico.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Ohio River flowing west to the Mississippi.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Missouri River crossing the northern plains.
trap_notes.p4: That is the main stem of the Mississippi River.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Great Plains, the semi-arid grassland biome east of the Rocky Mountains.
explanation: The Great Plains lie in the rain shadow east of the Rockies, supporting vast grasslands and commercial grain agriculture.

trap_notes.default: Look in the dry interior west of the Mississippi River.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Pacific coastline.
trap_notes.p3: That is the humid Florida Peninsula.
trap_notes.p4: That is the humid Atlantic Coastal Plain.

prompt: Select the pin on the Yellow River, which carries fertile loess silt across northern China.
explanation: The Yellow River (Huang He) makes a distinctive northern loop through the Loess Plateau before emptying into the Yellow Sea.

trap_notes.default: Look for the northernmost of China's two major rivers.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Yangtze River further south.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan rim.
trap_notes.p4: That is the Korean Peninsula.

prompt: Select the pin on the Yangtze River, Asia's longest river and a vital corridor to the East China Sea.
explanation: The Yangtze flows eastward across central China to the East China Sea, supporting dense populations and rice farming.

trap_notes.default: Look for the major river south of the Yellow River flowing east to the coast.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Yellow River to the north.
trap_notes.p3: That is Honshu in the Japanese archipelago.
trap_notes.p4: That is Hainan Island off southern China.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Tibetan Plateau, the high-elevation source of Asia's great rivers.
explanation: Bordered by the Himalayas, the Tibetan Plateau averages over 4,500 meters high and feeds both the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers.

trap_notes.default: Look in the far southwest along the dashed mountain ridge.
trap_notes.p2: That is the island of Taiwan.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Korean Peninsula.
trap_notes.p4: That is Hokkaido in northern Japan.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Korean Peninsula, which separates the Yellow Sea from the Sea of Japan.
explanation: The Korean Peninsula extends southward from northeastern China between the Yellow Sea on the west and the Sea of Japan on the east.

trap_notes.default: Find the peninsula jutting southward from the Asian mainland toward Japan.
trap_notes.p2: That is Honshu, Japan's main island.
trap_notes.p3: That is Taiwan off southeastern China.
trap_notes.p4: That is Hainan Island in the South China Sea.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Sea of Japan, enclosed by the Asian mainland and the Japanese islands.
explanation: The Sea of Japan lies between the Korean Peninsula and Russia on the west and the Japanese archipelago on the east.

trap_notes.default: Look between the Korean Peninsula and the main island of Japan.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Yellow Sea west of Korea.
trap_notes.p3: That is the East China Sea between China and Kyushu.
trap_notes.p4: That is the South China Sea.

prompt: Select the pin marking Taiwan, the mountainous island separated from southeastern China by a narrow strait.
explanation: Taiwan sits along the Tropic of Cancer off southeastern China, between the East China Sea and the South China Sea.

trap_notes.default: Look just off the southeastern coast of mainland China.
trap_notes.p2: That is Kyushu in southern Japan.
trap_notes.p3: That is Hainan Island further southwest.
trap_notes.p4: That is Hokkaido in northern Japan.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Strait of Malacca, the busy shipping lane between the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
explanation: The Strait of Malacca runs between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, carrying a huge share of East-West maritime trade.

trap_notes.default: Look in the far east of the map between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Strait of Hormuz at the Persian Gulf.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the Red Sea.
trap_notes.p4: That is the island of Sri Lanka south of India.

explanation: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, carrying roughly a fifth of global petroleum trade.

trap_notes.default: Look at the narrow mouth of the Persian Gulf northeast of Arabia.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern Red Sea.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Strait of Malacca in Southeast Asia.
trap_notes.p4: That is the shallow strait between India and Sri Lanka.

explanation: The Bab el-Mandeb separates the Arabian Peninsula from the Horn of Africa, forming the southern chokepoint of the Suez shipping route.

trap_notes.default: Look between southwestern Arabia and the Horn of Africa.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Strait of Hormuz at the Persian Gulf.
trap_notes.p3: That is Madagascar off southeastern Africa.
trap_notes.p4: That is the Strait of Malacca in Southeast Asia.

prompt: Select the pin marking the Ganges River Delta, the world's largest river delta on the Bay of Bengal.
explanation: Fed by Himalayan snowmelt and monsoon rains, the Ganges and Brahmaputra form a vast, densely populated delta on the Bay of Bengal.

trap_notes.default: Look on the eastern side of the Indian subcontinent at the head of the Bay of Bengal.
trap_notes.p2: That is the Indus River mouth on the Arabian Sea.
trap_notes.p3: That is the interior Deccan Plateau of southern India.
trap_notes.p4: That is the Persian Gulf.

explanation: The Indus flows southwest through arid plains into the Arabian Sea, supporting one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

trap_notes.p2: That is the Ganges River basin flowing southeast.
trap_notes.p3: That is the Horn of Africa.
trap_notes.p4: That is the island of Java in Indonesia.

prompt: Select the pin marking Madagascar, the large island off southeastern Africa known for unique wildlife.
explanation: Long geographic isolation from mainland Africa allowed Madagascar to evolve distinct endemic species such as lemurs.

trap_notes.default: Look in the southwestern Indian Ocean just east of Africa.
trap_notes.p2: That is Sri Lanka off southern India.
trap_notes.p3: That is Sumatra in Indonesia.
trap_notes.p4: That is Java in Indonesia.

items.text: Prolonged drought ruining local farms
Higher-paying factory jobs in a city
Civil war forcing families to flee
Strong public universities and clinics

prompt: Sort each migration driver into Push Factor or Pull Factor.
explanation: Push factors drive people away from a home area due to hardship, while pull factors attract migrants to a new destination.

trap_notes.default: Ask whether the factor drives someone out of home (push) or draws them toward a destination (pull).

items.text: Deep natural harbor with bedrock
Located along a busy transoceanic route
Flat floodplain above river rapids
Connected by rail to inland farm towns

prompt: Classify each urban feature as an example of Site or Situation.
explanation: Site describes the physical traits of a place itself, whereas situation describes its location relative to surrounding places.

trap_notes.default: Site is on-the-ground physical terrain; situation is external connectivity to other places.

items.text: Solar radiation captured by panels
Coal formed over millions of years
Wind turning offshore turbine blades
Crude oil pumped from shale basins

prompt: Sort each energy source into Renewable Resource or Nonrenewable Resource.
explanation: Renewable resources replenish naturally on human timescales, while fossil fuels form over millions of years and are finite.

trap_notes.default: Check whether the source replenishes continuously or exists in a finite geologic stock.

items.text: Preserves compass angles for navigation
Preserves true land size across latitudes
Makes Greenland look as large as Africa
Distorts shapes near poles to keep area

prompt: Match each map trait to Mercator Projection or Equal-Area Projection.
explanation: Mercator maps preserve direction and shape at the cost of huge polar area distortion; equal-area maps keep relative land sizes accurate.

trap_notes.default: Mercator is conformal (angles/navigation); equal-area sacrifices shape to keep true size.

items.text: Corn Belt defined by shared farm output
Metro area served by one commuter rail
State defined by legal tax boundaries
Delivery zone radiating from a warehouse

prompt: Classify each geographic area as a Formal Region or Functional Region.
explanation: Formal regions share a uniform trait throughout, while functional regions are organized around a central node and its connections.

trap_notes.default: Look for uniform shared traits (formal) versus a hub-and-spoke network (functional).

items.text: Afternoon thunderstorm passing a town
30-year average summer rainfall pattern
Cold front dropping temperatures tonight
Dry subtropical conditions in a desert

prompt: Sort each atmospheric description into Weather or Climate.
explanation: Weather refers to short-term atmospheric conditions, while climate describes long-term patterns averaged over decades.

trap_notes.default: Short-term events are weather; multi-decade averages and biome patterns are climate.

items.text: Mid-ocean ridge forming new seafloor
Deep ocean trench where plates subduct
East African rift valley pulling apart
Himalayan peaks pushed up by collision

prompt: Match each landform to a Divergent Boundary or Convergent Boundary.
explanation: Divergent boundaries pull plates apart to form rifts and ridges; convergent boundaries push plates together into trenches and mountains.

trap_notes.default: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries and collide or subduct at convergent boundaries.

items.text: Ice wedging splitting granite cracks
Acidic rainwater dissolving limestone
Tree roots prying apart sandstone
Oxygen rusting iron-rich rock layers

prompt: Classify each rock-breakdown process as Physical Weathering or Chemical Weathering.
explanation: Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals; chemical weathering alters rock composition.

trap_notes.default: Mechanical force (ice, roots) is physical; reactions (dissolving, rusting) are chemical.

items.text: Large mechanized wheat farms for export
Small plots feeding one extended family
High capital investment in fertilizers
High share of household labor by hand

prompt: Sort each agricultural trait into Commercial Farming or Subsistence Farming.
explanation: Commercial farming produces crops for sale using capital and machinery, while subsistence farming feeds the farmer's household.

trap_notes.default: Compare market-oriented, mechanized production with household-consumption farming.

items.text: High-rise apartments near subway stops
Scattered farmsteads miles apart
Mixed-use blocks walkable on foot
Extensive pastures and timberland

prompt: Classify each land-use pattern as High-Density Urban or Low-Density Rural.
explanation: Urban cores concentrate people, transit, and vertical buildings, whereas rural landscapes spread residences across farmland and open space.

trap_notes.default: Concentrated housing and transit belong to urban cores; dispersed farms are rural.

items.text: Moist ocean air rises and cools
Dry air descends and warms rapidly
Lush temperate forest receives rain
Rain shadow creates arid steppe

prompt: Sort each mountain-climate trait into Windward Slope or Leeward Slope.
explanation: Air forced up the windward side cools and drops rain, leaving dry descending air to form a rain shadow on the leeward side.

trap_notes.default: Wet rising air hits the windward side; dry descending air creates the leeward rain shadow.

items.text: Farmworkers moving from inland to coast
Nurses relocating to a foreign country
Retirees moving to a warmer home state
Refugees crossing a sovereign border

prompt: Classify each move as Internal Migration or International Migration.
explanation: Internal migration occurs within one country's borders, whereas international migration crosses between sovereign states.

trap_notes.default: Check whether the mover crosses an international border or stays within one nation.

items.text: Iron ore mining in open pits
Retail banking and customer lending
Commercial coastal fishing fleets
Hospital care and outpatient clinics

prompt: Sort each economic activity into the Primary Sector or Tertiary Sector.
explanation: The primary sector extracts raw materials directly from Earth, while the tertiary sector provides services to consumers and businesses.

trap_notes.default: Resource extraction is primary; services like banking and healthcare are tertiary.

items.text: Glacial erosion carving U-shaped valleys
Spread of official languages by trade
Monsoon wind shifts over South Asia
Zoning laws shaping suburban neighborhoods

prompt: Classify each topic under Physical Geography or Human Geography.
explanation: Physical geography examines natural landforms and climate, while human geography studies cultures, populations, and cities.

trap_notes.default: Natural Earth processes belong to physical geography; human institutions belong to human geography.

items.text: 30 degrees north, 90 degrees west
Two miles downstream from the bridge
Exact street address on a city grid
A three-hour drive north of the port

prompt: Sort each description into Absolute Location or Relative Location.
explanation: Absolute location uses fixed coordinates or addresses, whereas relative location describes a place in relation to other landmarks.

trap_notes.default: Fixed coordinates and addresses are absolute; descriptions using nearby landmarks are relative.

items.text: Viral song spreading outward online
Immigrants opening a homeland bakery
Solar panels adopted by neighboring towns
Settlers carrying a dialect to an island

prompt: Classify each cultural spread into Expansion Diffusion or Relocation Diffusion.
explanation: Expansion diffusion spreads an idea outward while staying strong at its origin; relocation diffusion occurs when people physically move.

trap_notes.default: Ideas spreading person-to-person are expansion; traits carried by migrating people are relocation.

items.text: Nearly circular territory around capital
Archipelago spread across many islands
Short distances from center to borders
Territory split by another country

prompt: Match each territorial trait to a Compact State or Fragmented State.
explanation: Compact states have roughly equidistant borders from their center, while fragmented states consist of disconnected pieces or islands.

trap_notes.default: Circular, unified territories are compact; island chains or separated exclaves are fragmented.

items.text: Dense multi-layered evergreen canopy
High daily temperature swings at night
Heavy year-round equatorial rainfall
Deep-rooted shrubs and waxy cacti

prompt: Sort each ecological trait into Tropical Rainforest or Hot Desert Biome.
explanation: Equatorial rainforests get heavy year-round rain and dense canopies, while deserts have sparse plants and wide daily temperature swings.

trap_notes.default: Equatorial moisture builds canopies; arid high-pressure belts produce wide temperature swings.

items.text: Total people divided by total land area
Total people divided by arable farmland
Includes uninhabited desert in denominator
Measures pressure on food-growing land

prompt: Match each population measure to Arithmetic Density or Physiological Density.
explanation: Arithmetic density uses all land area, whereas physiological density uses only arable land to gauge food-production pressure.

trap_notes.default: Arithmetic uses total land; physiological narrows the denominator to farmable land.

items.text: Contour lines showing elevation changes
Shaded counties showing median income
Streams, cliffs, and hiking trail grades
Dot symbols showing coffee production

prompt: Classify each map feature under Topographic Map or Thematic Map.
explanation: Topographic maps show terrain elevation using contour lines, while thematic maps visualize a specific social or natural variable.

trap_notes.default: Elevation and terrain contours are topographic; single-variable data overlays are thematic.

items.text: Shows individual city blocks and alleys
Shows an entire continent on one page
Uses a ratio such as 1:10,000
Uses a ratio such as 1:50,000,000

prompt: Sort each cartographic trait into Large-Scale Map or Small-Scale Map.
explanation: Large-scale maps zoom in on small areas in high detail (larger fraction), while small-scale maps zoom out to show vast regions.

trap_notes.default: Think of the ratio as a fraction: 1/10,000 is larger than 1/50,000,000 and shows more detail.

items.text: Border following a winding river channel
Border drawn along the 49th parallel
Border running along a mountain crest
Straight-line desert border on a map

prompt: Classify each border type as a Natural Boundary or Geometric Boundary.
explanation: Natural boundaries follow rivers or mountain ridges, while geometric boundaries use straight lines or latitude and longitude.

trap_notes.default: Landforms like rivers and ridges are natural; straight surveyed lines are geometric.

items.text: National rail network linking regions
Regional separatist movement in hills
Shared civic holidays and constitution
Severe wealth gap between provinces

prompt: Sort each political factor into Centripetal Force or Centrifugal Force.
explanation: Centripetal forces unite a state and strengthen stability, whereas centrifugal forces divide citizens and weaken central authority.

trap_notes.default: Centripetal pulls a country together; centrifugal pushes regions or groups apart.

items.text: Fresh dairy and leafy market greens
Extensive cattle ranching on cheap land
High transport cost per day of spoilage
Dry wheat stored and shipped in bulk

prompt: Match each Von Thunen land-use trait to the Near-City Zone or Outer-Ring Zone.
explanation: In Von Thunen's model, perishable goods cluster near the urban market, while grain and ranching occupy cheaper outer land.

trap_notes.default: Perishable, high-value goods sit close to the city; space-hungry ranching and grain sit farther out.

items.text: Most workers employed in service jobs
Large share of workforce in farming
Low infant mortality and long lifespan
Rapid population growth and young median age

prompt: Sort each demographic indicator into High-Income Economy or Low-Income Economy.
explanation: High-income economies feature service jobs and long lifespans, whereas low-income economies have younger populations and more farming.

trap_notes.default: Compare service-sector, aging societies with agrarian, fast-growing populations.

items.text: Unusually warm central Pacific surface
Unusually cool equatorial Pacific water
Weakened trade winds off South America
Stronger trade winds pushing water west

prompt: Classify each Pacific Ocean condition under El Nino Phase or La Nina Phase.
explanation: El Nino brings warmer Pacific waters and weaker trade winds, whereas La Nina brings cooler eastern Pacific waters and stronger trade winds.

trap_notes.default: El Nino is the warm phase with weaker trades; La Nina is the cool phase with stronger trades.

items.text: Driven mainly by global prevailing winds
Driven by cold, salty water sinking
Forms large rotating ocean gyres
Slowly circulates along the abyssal floor

prompt: Sort each ocean-circulation trait into Surface Current or Deep Ocean Current.
explanation: Prevailing winds drive surface gyres, while temperature and salinity differences power deep thermohaline ocean circulation.

trap_notes.default: Winds move surface gyres; water density (temperature and salinity) drives deep currents.

items.text: Rural families moving into dense cities
City residents moving to outer car suburbs
Rising share of national population in cities
Single-family subdivisions replacing farms

prompt: Classify each settlement trend as Urbanization or Suburbanization.
explanation: Urbanization shifts population from rural areas into cities, whereas suburbanization spreads city dwellers outward into lower-density rings.

trap_notes.default: Rural-to-city growth is urbanization; city-to-outer-ring sprawl is suburbanization.

items.text: Managing forests for sustainable timber
Banning logging in wilderness parks
Regulating river dams for long-term use
Keeping ecosystems untouched by industry

prompt: Sort each environmental approach into Conservation or Preservation.
explanation: Conservation promotes planned, sustainable use of natural resources, whereas preservation protects nature from human extraction altogether.

trap_notes.default: Wise sustainable use is conservation; strict hands-off protection is preservation.

items.text: Wastewater pipe draining from one factory
Fertilizer runoff washing off many farms
Oil leaking from a single damaged tanker
Road salt carried by rain across streets

prompt: Classify each water-pollution example as Point-Source or Nonpoint-Source.
explanation: Point-source pollution enters waterways from a single identifiable pipe or site, while nonpoint-source pollution comes from diffuse runoff.

trap_notes.default: One identifiable outlet is point-source; wide surface runoff from many areas is nonpoint-source.
